h.strategy: Use retrieved findings to identify which settings are strong, weak or neutral, and which parts can be cut off from the outcome by other settings. Build hypotheses mainly from (a) the edited field's current value in the parent, since replacing a strong value with a weak one hurts and filling an empty or harmful slot helps, and (b) conditions that disconnect the edited part, which shrink its effect. When finding flaws, replace any hypothesis whose direction could plausibly reverse because of a competing effect, or whose mechanism relies on partial redundancy between different parts. Ensure varied edit fields and values. State a one-sentence mechanism.

hyps.why: Giving node 1 its first input via a strong conv activates a whole branch, a bigger gain than upgrading an existing op.
Connecting node 1 to the input with a useful conv activates the node-1 branch, which beats modifying an existing op.
With no input into node 1, edge 4 carries no signal, so upgrading it barely matters.
Edge 2 starts at node 1, which is disconnected from the input when edge 0 is none, so the edit has almost no effect.
Without input to node 1, edge 2 passes nothing, so strengthening it has little effect.
With edge 5 removed, node 2 is cut off from the output, so a stronger op on edge 2 has little effect.
Filling an empty direct input-to-output edge with the strongest op gives a larger gain than replacing an op that already carries signal.
Filling the empty edge into the output with a strong conv helps more than upgrading an existing op.
An identity shortcut to the output is worth much more when the slot was empty than when it replaces an existing op.
Removing edge 4 when node 1 has no input removes a dead edge at no cost, whereas otherwise it loses a live path.
